docs.title: nixos-homelab-media
docs.text:
A self-hosted media stack on top of nixos-homelab: Plex plus the usual *Arr suite for automated acquisition, wired together with API keys and download-client registrations handled automatically.

For the full list of module options, see the options reference.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
{
  inputs = {
    ...
    homelab-media = {
      url = "github:nixos-homelab/media";
      inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";
    };
    ...
  };
}

{ inputs, ... }:
{
  imports = [
    inputs.homelab-media.nixosModules.sonarr
    inputs.homelab-media.nixosModules.radarr
  ];
  config = {
    homelab.sonarr.enable = true;
    homelab.radarr.enable = true;
  };
}

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
• plex: Plex Media Server.
  • sonarr / radarr: TV and movie collection management.
  • prowlarr: indexer management, auto-registered with Sonarr/Radarr.
  • flood: web UI and download client for rtorrent, auto-registered with Sonarr/Radarr/Prowlarr.
  • rtorrent: the torrent daemon flood drives, optionally routed through homelab-networking's privacy-vpn.
  • sabnzbd: Usenet download client, auto-registered the same way as flood.

docs.title: lib.integration.mkArrStackIntegrationScript
docs.text: Build a shell script that idempotently registers an integration with an *Arr-stack app's (Sonarr/Radarr/Prowlarr-style) REST API: it checks apiEndpoint for an existing entry matching settings.implementation, and if none is found, POSTs settings to create one.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
name (String): Name of the app being integrated with, used in log messages

apiEndpoint (String): URL of the integration list/create endpoint

authApiKeyVar (String): Environment variable holding the API key for apiEndpoint

settings (AttrSet): The integration payload to POST; settings.fields is an attrset serialized to the API's field-list format, and settings.implementation identifies the integration type

apiKeyFieldName (String): Field name to inject apiKeyVar's value under in settings.fields (optional, required if apiKeyVar is set)

apiKeyVar (String): Environment variable to inject into settings.fields (optional)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
integration.mkArrStackIntegrationScript {
  name = "Sonarr";
  apiEndpoint = "http://prowlarr.prowlarr:9696/api/v1/applications";
  authApiKeyVar = "PROWLARR_API_KEY";
  apiKeyFieldName = "apiKey";
  apiKeyVar = "SONARR_API_KEY";
  settings = {
    implementation = "Sonarr";
    fields.baseUrl = "http://sonarr.sonarr:8989";
  };
}

docs.title: nixos-homelab-monitoring
docs.text:
Observability stack on top of nixos-homelab: Grafana, long-term metrics storage, and the exporters/collectors that feed it, for both cluster and host-level monitoring.

For the full list of module options, see the options reference.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
{
  inputs = {
    ...
    homelab-monitoring = {
      url = "github:nixos-homelab/monitoring";
      inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";
    };
    ...
  };
}

{ inputs, ... }:
{
  imports = [
    inputs.homelab-monitoring.nixosModules.grafana
    inputs.homelab-monitoring.nixosModules.mimir
  ];
  config = {
    homelab.grafana.enable = true;
    homelab.mimir.enable = true;
  };
}

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
• grafana: dashboards, provisioned with datasources for Mimir.
  • mimir: long-term Prometheus-compatible metrics storage.
  • alloy: the Grafana Alloy agent that scrapes and forwards metrics/logs, with a per-service integrations allow-list like homepage's.
  • node-exporter: host-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network).
  • smartctl-exporter: disk S.M.A.R.T. health metrics.
  • zfs-exporter: ZFS pool metrics.

docs.title: nixos-homelab-networking
docs.text:
The networking base that ties the rest of the homelab together. Every workload across every nixos-homelab-* repo declares allowIngress/ allowEgress on its kubenix workload -- this repo's cilium module is what actually enforces them as network policy; without it they're just labels. It also provides the CNI itself, inbound and outbound VPNs, routable IP pools, and DNS management.

See the Cilium network policies docs for the policies this repo's cilium module gives kubenix pods and lib.toPorts, and the options reference for the full list of module options.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
{
  inputs = {
    ...
    homelab-networking = {
      url = "github:nixos-homelab/networking";
      inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";
    };
    ...
  };
}

{ inputs, ... }:
{
  imports = [ inputs.homelab-networking.nixosModules.cilium ];
  config.homelab.cilium.enable = true;
}

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
• cilium: the Cilium CNI, plus the LoadBalancer IP pool it hands out from -- see the Cilium network policies docs for the policies it gives the pods of kubenix submodules.
  • routed-ippool: a routable IPv4 pool for LoadBalancer services, routed to the cluster from the LAN.
  • client-vpn: the inbound WireGuard gateway -- named access groups, each scoped to specific services or full cluster access, for remote kubectl/service access.
  • privacy-vpn: an outbound WireGuard tunnel to an external VPN provider, for routing a workload's egress traffic through it (e.g. homelab-media's rtorrent).
  • external-dns: external-dns, managing DNS records for cluster services automatically.
  • unifi: Unifi Network Controller, for managing Ubiquiti networking gear.
  • netutils: a debugging container with common networking tools, for troubleshooting from inside the cluster.

docs.title: Cilium network policies
docs.text: The policies of kubenix pods, the Cilium types and lib.toPorts.

docs.title: kubenix pods
docs.text:
The policies of the CNI-neutral intent of every instance of a submodule that runs pods, or of pods (the feature pod-policy), added through kubenix submodules.defaults when homelab.cilium.enable is set. They select the pods by app.kubernetes.io/name of the instance, or the selector of pods:

  • policyPorts, all of ports unless set: pods labeled cluster.local/<name>-egress: allow in any namespace may reach them, through the CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy pod-to-<name> and the CiliumNetworkPolicy <name>-from-pod.
  • apiServerPorts: the API server may reach them, <name>-from-apiserver.
  • worldPorts: the world outside the cluster may reach them, <name>-from-world.

They go in the manifest of the instance; change them through its config, as kubernetes.resources.ciliumNetworkPolicies.<name>-from-pod.

docs.title: Cilium types
docs.text: nixosModules.cilium-crds (which cilium imports) adds the kubenix types of the Cilium CRDs, of the version of the chart cilium installs, and hands the CRDs to the manifests check through homelab.cluster.runtimeCRDs, as Cilium's operator creates them at runtime. It deploys nothing: a module that writes Cilium policies by hand imports it, so it evaluates with Cilium off too.

docs.title: lib.toPorts
docs.text:
Cilium's toPorts from a flat list of ports as a NetworkPolicy writes them, for policies written by hand: port numbers, or { port; protocol; } (and endPort). Cilium wants the port as a string. No ports give null, which leaves the field out.

homelab.kubernetes.kubernetes.resources.ciliumNetworkPolicies.dns.spec.egress = [
  {
    toEntities = [ "world" ];
    toPorts = inputs.homelab-networking.lib.toPorts [
      { port = 53; protocol = "UDP"; }
      443
    ];
  }
];

gives toPorts = [ { ports = [ { port = "53"; protocol = "UDP"; } { port = "443"; } ]; } ].

docs.title: nixos-homelab-shared
docs.text:
Every other nixos-homelab-* repo takes this one as an input and builds on its cluster module, the facts of the cluster, with a runner that runs it: the k3s module, enabled. It also provides shared services used across those repos: a dashboard, TLS, and SSH-key access to the cluster. Databases and storage are in nixos-homelab-storage.

See the kubenix docs for the typed resources and submodules of homelab.kubernetes, and the options reference for the full list of module options.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
{
  inputs = {
    ...
    homelab-shared = {
      url = "github:nixos-homelab/shared";
      inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";
    };
    ...
  };
}

{ inputs, ... }:
{
  imports = [ inputs.homelab-shared.nixosModules.k3s ];
  config.homelab.k3s.enable = true;
}

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
• cluster: the shared homelab.cluster.* options every other module in this ecosystem builds on, whichever runner runs the cluster: IP families, pod/service CIDRs, debug tools, backup aggregation, the images to preload and the manifests to apply, and the facts the runner sets (kubeconfig, unit, Kubernetes version).
  • k3s: runs the cluster on k3s (homelab.k3s): it imports cluster, preloads its images, applies its manifests, and drains the node at shutdown.
  • workloads: the settings every workload shares (homelab.workloads: domain, gateway class, ACME issuer, pod user and group) and kubenix configuration in homelab.kubernetes, with the workload submodule -- see the kubenix docs. cluster imports it and hands what it holds to the runner.
  • homepage: the homepage dashboard, with a per-service integrations allow-list.
  • cert-manager: cert-manager plus a LibDNS ACME webhook, for automated TLS certificates.
  • k8sss: deploys k8sss for SSH-key-based kubectl access.

docs.title: kubenix
docs.text: The workloads module holds the settings every workload shares, in homelab.workloads (domain, gatewayClassName, acmeProvider, containerUtils, securityContext), and the submodules below. homelab.kubernetes takes kubenix configuration of the cluster: typed Kubernetes resources, so a misspelled field fails at evaluation and names where it was set. Each submodule instance goes to the runner as a manifest of its own, named after the instance; the other objects go to the manifest kubenix.

docs.title: Custom resources
docs.text:
The custom resources are typed too, from the CRDs: lib.crd2types.customTypes turns a CustomResourceDefinition into kubenix customTypes, at evaluation, so a bump of a CRD retypes its resources. This module types Gateway API's experimental channel, as pinned in lib.crds.pinned; the cert-manager module adds those of its chart, and the module of the CNI its own (networking's cilium-crds). Every submodule gets them. Their attribute names are kubenix's: the plural cased like the kind (gateways, hTTPRoutes, ciliumNetworkPolicies, certificates, clusterIssuers). Optional fields default to null and are left out; value validations (patterns, bounds, CEL rules) stay with the API server. A list the CRD merges by one key takes an attribute set by that key, like the lists kubenix keys in its core types: Gateway listeners by name, so an instance changes one listener of its Gateway (mkForce where the workload sets the field already):

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.grafana.config.kubernetes.resources.gateways.grafana.spec.listeners.grafana.port =
  lib.mkForce 8443;

A list still works there; its items keep their order, ahead of those given by key. A CRD that starts using a schema construct crd2types doesn't know fails evaluation, naming where.

homelab.kubernetes.kubernetes.resources.certificates.plex = {
  metadata.namespace = "plex";
  spec = {
    secretName = "plex-tls";
    dnsNames = [ "plex.example.org" ];
    issuerRef = { kind = "ClusterIssuer"; name = "letsencrypt-production"; };
  };
};

A module adds the types of a CRD it installs to homelab.kubernetes.kubernetes.customTypes. Cluster-scoped resources need metadata.namespace = null.

docs.title: workload
docs.text:
A long-running workload: a Namespace and a Deployment named after the instance, and depending on the args a PersistentVolumeClaim, a Service and a Gateway with its HTTPRoutes.

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.grafana = {
  submodule = "workload";
  args = {
    allowEgress = [ "internet" "mimir" "postgresql" ];
    dataPath = "/var/lib/grafana";
    ingressPort = 3000;
    ports.web = 3000;
    container = {
      image = "grafana:latest";
      env = [ { name = "GF_PATHS_DATA"; value = "/var/lib/grafana"; } ];
    };
  };
};
  • container: the main container, named after the instance, as kubenix's Container type. It's locked down by default (allowPrivilegeEscalation = false, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, NET_BIND_SERVICE added when it has ports); set securityContext.capabilities.add for more.
  • ports: the container ports by name, a port number or { containerPort; protocol; }. They also make the Service, with the same names.
  • dataPath: a 1Gi PersistentVolumeClaim named after the workload, mounted here in the main container.
  • ingressPort: a Gateway at <gateway.subdomain>.<gateway.domain> (the bare domain when gateway.subdomain = null) routing to this Service port, with a redirect from HTTP; allows ingress from gateway. httpRouteRules go ahead of the catch-all rule.
  • policyPorts: the names of the ports other pods may reach, all of them by default; see below.
  • apiServerPorts, worldPorts: the names of the ports the API server and the world outside the cluster may reach, none by default.
  • allowIngress/allowEgress: the pod labels cluster.local/<workload>-ingress/-egress: allow, for the label selectors of the network policies.

The workload holds no network policies of its own, only this intent (policy.nix). The module of the CNI turns it into policies for every instance with the feature pod-policy through submodules.defaults: networking's cilium lets pods labeled cluster.local/<workload>-egress: allow reach the policyPorts, and so on. Without a CNI module there are none. - securityContext: runAsUser, runAsGroup (also the fsGroup) and supplementalGroups of the pod. They default to homelab.workloads.securityContext, as gateway.domain, gateway.className and gateway.issuer default to the domain, gatewayClassName and acmeProvider there.

Anything else goes on the instance config, where the objects are kubenix resources. Lists kubenix keys by name (containers, volumes, ports) take attribute sets:

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.unifi.config.kubernetes.resources = {
  services.unifi.spec.type = "LoadBalancer";
  deployments.unifi.spec.template.spec.volumes.config.hostPath.path = "/srv/unifi";
};

pod-spec.nix holds the main container and the pod security context for every submodule that runs pods; submodules.defaults with features = [ "pod-spec" ] reaches all of them.

docs.title: deployment, daemonset, job, cronjob, script
docs.text:
The pod alone, in the resource that runs it, named after the instance: container, ports, policyPorts, apiServerPorts, worldPorts, allowIngress, allowEgress and securityContext as in the workload, with no Namespace or Service. A Deployment is recreated on change; the pod of a Job or CronJob isn't restarted unless the instance sets restartPolicy. cronjob takes the schedule.

script runs a bash script once: a ConfigMap and a Job, the script mounted at a path hashed from it, so a changed script changes the pod template of the Job, the runner replaces the Job and it runs again. It runs in image, the container-utils of the cluster unless set.

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.backup-grafana-db = {
  submodule = "cronjob";
  args = {
    schedule = "10 3 * * *";
    allowEgress = [ "postgresql" ];
    container = {
      image = "postgresql:latest";
      command = [ "pg_dump" "--file=/dumps/grafana.pgdump" ];
      volumeMounts."/dumps".name = "dumps";
    };
  };
  config.kubernetes.resources.cronJobs.backup-grafana-db.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.volumes.dumps.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName =
    "database-dumps";
};

docs.title: service
docs.text:
A Service named after the instance, selecting the pods named so. ports by name: a port number, or the fields of a ServicePort.

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.alloy = {
  submodule = "service";
  args.ports.web = 3000;
};

docs.title: pods
docs.text:
The policy intent of pods something else runs (a release, a static manifest, another module): ports, policyPorts, apiServerPorts and worldPorts as in the workload, for the pods with the labels selector in the namespace of the instance, app.kubernetes.io/name of the instance name unless set. It writes no objects; the CNI module adds the policies as for any pod.

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.cert-manager.config.submodules.instances.webhook = {
  name = "cert-manager-webhook";
  submodule = "pods";
  args = {
    selector = {
      "app.kubernetes.io/name" = "webhook";
      "app.kubernetes.io/instance" = "cert-manager";
    };
    ports.https = 10250;
    apiServerPorts = [ "https" ];
  };
};

docs.title: manifest
docs.text:
Objects that go to the runner together: the resources on the instance config and the instances nested in it. Every top-level instance is one manifest, and the runner deletes what a manifest stops holding. An object that moves to another manifest is deleted when the runner applies the old manifest first, and a Namespace or a PersistentVolumeClaim takes what it holds with it. So objects that went to the runner together stay in one manifest, under the old name.

homelab.kubernetes.submodules.instances.cert-manager = {
  submodule = "manifest";
  config = {
    kubernetes.resources.namespaces.cert-manager.metadata.namespace = null;
    submodules.instances = {
      webhook = {
        name = "cert-manager-webhook-libdns";
        submodule = "deployment";
        args.container.image = "cert-manager-webhook-libdns:latest";
      };
      webhook-service = {
        name = "cert-manager-webhook-libdns";
        submodule = "service";
        args.ports.https = { port = 443; targetPort = 8443; };
      };
    };
  };
};

All submodules, workload and manifest included, put their objects in the namespace of the instance they're nested in, or the one named after the instance at the top; set config.kubernetes.namespace for another. Two nested instances whose objects share a name, like a Deployment and the Service in front of it, take keys of their own and the object name as name.

docs.title: lib.crd2types.customTypes
docs.text: The kubenix kubernetes.customTypes of a CustomResourceDefinition, one per served version, for kubernetes.customTypesModuleDefinesCRDSpec = false: each module types the fields of the resource besides apiVersion, kind and metadata, which kubenix types itself. Optional fields default to null, which kubenix leaves out. A list the API server merges by one key (x-kubernetes-list-type: map) is an attribute set by that key, as kubenix has it for its core types; a list still works there. docs.title: lib.images.pinned
docs.text: The upstream images pinned in a Dockerfile, as image archives for homelab.cluster.images. Dependabot bumps the FROM name:tag@digest lines; their Nix hashes are in images.lock next to the Dockerfile, which nix run github:nixos-homelab/shared#lock-images updates. The tag gets the digest's first 12 hex digits, so a bump changes the pod spec and rolls the workload. Each archive's ref is its name:tag.

in
{
  homelab.cluster.images = [ redis ];
  # ...
  image = redis.ref;
  imagePullPolicy = "Never";
}

docs.title: nixos-homelab-storage
docs.text:
Databases and persistent storage on top of nixos-homelab: the PostgreSQL and Redis instances that apps in the other repos keep their data in, PersistentVolumes on an NFS export, and Samba file sharing on the host.

For the full list of module options, see the options reference.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
{
  inputs = {
    ...
    homelab-storage = {
      url = "github:nixos-homelab/storage";
      inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";
    };
    ...
  };
}

{ inputs, ... }:
{
  imports = [ inputs.homelab-storage.nixosModules.postgresql ];
  config.homelab.postgresql = {
    enable = true;
    databases.myapp.backup.enable = true;
  };
}

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
• postgresql: a shared PostgreSQL instance with declarative database creation and backups.
  • redis: a shared Redis instance with a database-index registry, to keep workloads from colliding on the same DB number.
  • nfs-provisioner: a dynamic PersistentVolume provisioner backed by an NFS export.
  • smb: Samba file sharing, with per-user passwords set up through setup-secrets.
